187.stem:
A university uses gas to heat its buildings. Over a period of 10 weekdays during winter, the gas used each day was measured in megawatts (MW) and the average outside temperature each day was recorded in degrees Celsius (°C).

Using $x$ as the average daily outside temperature and $y$ as the total daily gas usage, the equation of the least-squares regression line was found.

The equation of the regression line predicts that when the temperature is $0^\circ\text{C}$, the daily gas usage is 236 MW.

The ten temperatures measured were: $0^\circ, 0^\circ, 0^\circ, 2^\circ, 5^\circ, 7^\circ, 8^\circ, 9^\circ, 9^\circ, 10^\circ$.

The total gas usage for the ten weekdays was 1840 MW.

In any bivariate dataset, the least-squares regression line passes through the point $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$, where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean of the $x$-values and $\bar{y}$ is the sample mean of the $y$-values.

figures.cap: blank grid: daily gas usage (MW) 160-240 against average daily outside temperature 0-10 °C

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\bar{x}&=\dfrac{0+0+0+2+5+7+8+9+9+10}{10}\\&=5\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ (\bar{x},\bar{y})=(5,184)$$

A class of 30 students sat an algebra test and a geometry test. The results were displayed in a scatterplot, and a line of best fit was drawn, as shown in the graph below.

parts.note: Bivariate data analysis (scatterplots, association) is not in the 2024 Advanced course · Standard: MST-12-S1-06

solutions.latex:
$$m = \dfrac{50 - 30}{80 - 40} = \dfrac{20}{40} = \dfrac{1}{2}$$

$$\therefore\ G = \dfrac{1}{2}A + 10$$

solutions.latex:
Using $m=\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$:
$$m_{AB}=\dfrac{6-3}{5+4}=\dfrac{3}{9}=\dfrac{1}{3}$$
$$m_{CD}=\dfrac{-2+1}{0-3}=\dfrac{-1}{-3}=\dfrac{1}{3}$$

solutions.latex:
Using the point-gradient form with $A(-4,\,3)$ and $m=\dfrac{1}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-3&=\dfrac{1}{3}(x+4)\\3y-9&=x+4\\x-3y+13&=0\end{aligned}$$
Or, using $B(5,\,6)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y-6&=\dfrac{1}{3}(x-5)\\3y-18&=x-5\\x-3y+13&=0\end{aligned}$$

Since $ED\perp AB$, $m_{ED}\times m_{AB}=-1$:
$$m_{ED}=-\dfrac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}=-3$$
Using $D(0,\,-2)$:
$$\begin{aligned}y+2&=-3(x-0)\\3x+y+2&=0\end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: perpendicular lines through (0,3) and (0,2) cutting the x-axis at L and M, LM = 5 [diagram not to scale]

solutions.latex:
$L$ is where $y=ax+3$ meets the $x$-axis: $ax+3=0$, so $x=-\dfrac{3}{a}$.

$M$ is where $y=bx+2$ meets the $x$-axis: $bx+2=0$, so $x=-\dfrac{2}{b}$.
$$\begin{aligned}LM&=-\dfrac{2}{b}-\left(-\dfrac{3}{a}\right)\\&=-\dfrac{2}{b}+\dfrac{3}{a}\end{aligned}$$
$LM=5$, and the lines are perpendicular, so $ab=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{2}{b}+\dfrac{3}{a}&=5\\3b-2a&=5ab &&(\text{multiply by } ab)\\3b-2a&=-5 &&\ldots(1)\end{aligned}$$
$$a=-\dfrac{1}{b}\quad\ldots(2)$$
Substituting (2) into (1):
$$\begin{aligned}3b-2\left(-\dfrac{1}{b}\right)&=-5\\3b+\dfrac{2}{b}&=-5\\3b^2+5b+2&=0\\(b+1)(3b+2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
$b=-1$ or $b=-\dfrac{2}{3}$, so
$$\begin{cases}a=1\\b=-1\end{cases}\text{ or }\begin{cases}a=\dfrac{3}{2}\\[6pt]b=-\dfrac{2}{3}\end{cases}$$
Since $a>1$, $a=\dfrac{3}{2}$ and $b=-\dfrac{2}{3}$:
$$a+b=\dfrac{3}{2}-\dfrac{2}{3}=\dfrac{5}{6}$$

parts.latex: Find the equation of the line through the midpoint of the interval from $A(3,2)$ to $B(-7,8)$ perpendicular to the line $\dfrac{x}{6}+\dfrac{y}{2}=1$.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Midpoint of }AB&=\left(\dfrac{3+(-7)}{2},\dfrac{2+8}{2}\right)\\&=(-2,5)\end{aligned}$$
Multiplying $\dfrac{x}{6}+\dfrac{y}{2}=1$ by 6:
$$\begin{aligned}x+3y&=6\\3y&=6-x\end{aligned}$$
so its gradient is $m=-\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Perpendicular lines have $m_1\times m_2=-1$:
$$m_\perp=3$$

$$\begin{aligned}y-5&=3(x+2)\\y&=3x+11\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Consider the simultaneous equations.

$$\begin{aligned}2ax+y-5&=0\\x+3y-2a&=0\end{aligned}$$

If the equations have no real solutions, what is the value of $a$?

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} 2ax+y-5 &= 0 && (1) \\ x+3y-2a &= 0 && (2) \end{aligned}$$

Make $y$ the subject:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{From (1)}: \ y &= -2ax+5 \\ \text{From (2)}: \ y &= -\dfrac{1}{3}x+\dfrac{2}{3}a \end{aligned}$$

Both are straight lines. No real solutions means no point of intersection, so the lines are parallel and have equal gradients:

$$\begin{aligned} -2a &= -\dfrac{1}{3} \\ a &= \dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The straight lines shown below $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ have equations $x+ay=b$ and $x+cy=d$ respectively. Which of the following are true?

I. $a<c$

II. $b>d$

III. $a+b<c+d$

\exfigure{1337_q10_1}

solutions.latex:
Write each line as $y=-\dfrac{1}{a}x+\dfrac{b}{a}$, so its gradient is $-\dfrac{1}{a}$ and its $y$-intercept is $\dfrac{b}{a}$. The other line has gradient $-\dfrac{1}{c}$ and $y$-intercept $\dfrac{d}{c}$.

Both lines have positive gradient, so $a<0$ and $c<0$.

Statement I: $\ell_2$ is steeper than $\ell_1$, so $\dfrac{1}{|c|}>\dfrac{1}{|a|}$, that is $|a|>|c|$. Since both are negative, $a<c$. True.

Statement II: for $\ell_1$ the $y$-intercept is $-1$, so $\dfrac{b}{a}=-1$ and $b=-a>0$.

$\ell_2$ crosses the $x$-axis left of the origin and rises, so its $y$-intercept $\dfrac{d}{c}$ is positive. With $c<0$ this gives $d<0$.

Hence $b>0>d$. True.

Statement III: $a+b=a+(-a)=0$, while $c+d$ is negative (both $c<0$ and $d<0$).

So $a+b>c+d$. False.

$$\therefore\ \text{I and II only}$$
Hence the correct option is A.

parts.latex: Show that the equation of diagonal $BD$ is $y = 3x - 9$.

The equation of diagonal $AC$ is $x + 3y = 23$.

Find the coordinates of $E$, the point of intersection of the diagonals.
Show that $E$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

solutions.latex:
The diagonal $BD$ passes through $B(7,12)$ and $D(2,-3)$.

The gradient is
$$\begin{aligned} m_{BD} &= \dfrac{-3 - 12}{2 - 7} \\ &= \dfrac{-15}{-5} \\ &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
Using point-gradient form with $B(7,12)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y - 12 &= 3(x - 7) \\ y - 12 &= 3x - 21 \\ y &= 3x - 9 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of $BD$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$E$ lies on both diagonals, so substitute $y = 3x - 9$ into $x + 3y = 23$.
$$\begin{aligned} x + 3(3x - 9) &= 23 \\ x + 9x - 27 &= 23 \\ 10x &= 50 \\ x &= 5 \end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 3\times 5 - 9 \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ E = (5, 6)$$

solutions.latex:
The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ passes through the midpoint of $AB$ with gradient perpendicular to $AB$.
$$\begin{aligned} m_{AB} &= \dfrac{12 - 8}{7 - (-1)} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{8} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
So the gradient of the perpendicular bisector is $-2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Midpoint of } AB &= \left(\dfrac{-1+7}{2}, \dfrac{8+12}{2}\right) \\ &= (3, 10) \end{aligned}$$
The perpendicular bisector is
$$\begin{aligned} y - 10 &= -2(x - 3) \\ y - 10 &= -2x + 6 \\ 2x + y - 16 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Test $E(5,6)$:
$$2(5) + 6 - 16 = 0$$
Hence $E$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

parts.latex:
The number plane below shows the interval joining the points $A(-5, -4)$ and $B(-1, -3)$.

The line, $l$, is drawn through $B$ so as to be perpendicular to $AB$ and meets the $x$-axis at $C$ and the $y$-axis at $D$.

solutions.latex:
Gradient of $AB$:
$$m_{AB} = \dfrac{-3-(-4)}{-1-(-5)} = \dfrac14$$
The line $l$ is perpendicular to $AB$, so $m_l = -4$.

It passes through $B(-1,-3)$, so use $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$.
$$\begin{aligned} y + 3 &= -4(x+1) \\ y &= -4x - 7 \end{aligned}$$
Point $D$ is the $y$-intercept, so $D$ is $(0,-7)$.

Point $C$ is where $y = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -4x - 7 \\ x &= -\dfrac74 \end{aligned}$$
So $C$ is $\left(-\dfrac74, 0\right)$.

Triangle $COD$ is right-angled at $O$, with $OD = 7$ and $OC = \dfrac74$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac12 \times \dfrac74 \times 7 \\ &= \dfrac{49}{8} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the gradient of the line $3x + 4y + 5 = 0$

solutions.latex:
Rearrange to the form $y = mx + c$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4y &= -3x - 5 \\ y &= -\dfrac{3}{4}x - \dfrac{5}{4} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient is $-\dfrac{3}{4}$, which is option A.

parts.latex: Which line is perpendicular to $3x+4y+7=0$?

solutions.latex:
Rearrange $3x+4y+7=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}4y&=-3x-7\\y&=-\dfrac{3}{4}x-\dfrac{7}{4}\end{aligned}$$
So $m=-\dfrac{3}{4}$ and the perpendicular gradient is $m_\perp=\dfrac{4}{3}$.

Option C:
$$\begin{aligned}6y&=8x-7\\y&=\dfrac{4}{3}x-\dfrac{7}{6}\end{aligned}$$
The gradient is $\dfrac{4}{3}$, so the answer is option C.

parts.latex: Let $M$ be the mid point of $(-1,4)$ and $(5,8)$. Then, the equation of line through $M$ with gradient $\dfrac{-1}{2}$ is:

solutions.latex:
The midpoint is $M(2,6)$.

The line through $M$ with gradient $-\dfrac{1}{2}$ is:

parts.latex: Solve the double inequation $-3 \le 3x - 2 < 4$ and write your answer using “bracket interval notation”.

solutions.latex:
Do the same operation to every part of the inequality, one operation per line.
$$\begin{aligned} -3&\le 3x-2<4\\ -1&\le 3x<6 &&(\text{add } 2)\\ -\dfrac{1}{3}&\le x<2 &&(\text{divide by } 3)\end{aligned}$$
In interval notation the solution is
$$\left[-\dfrac{1}{3},\,2\right)$$

parts.latex: Which of the following correctly expresses $y$ as the subject of the formula $2x-5y+3=0$?

solutions.latex:
Rearrange to make $y$ the subject.
$$\begin{aligned} 2x-5y+3&=0\\ 5y&=2x+3\\ y&=\dfrac{2}{5}x+\dfrac{3}{5} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option C.
